question.question: According to Section 3, what is the definition of on-machine measurement?
expected_points: The measurement target is located within the machine tool workspace.
The measurement device is within or nearby the machine tool workspace.

answer.content: According to Section 3, on-machine measurement is defined as a measurement performed where the measurement target is located within the machine tool workspace and the measurement device is within or nearby the machine tool workspace [4].

question.question: What benefits and limitations of on-machine measurement does the document describe compared with a stand-alone CMM?
expected_points: OMM can reduce machining time, scrap, rework, manual intervention and the second-fixation problem.
The machine tool environment has variable temperature, humidity and particulate matter, so OMM is generally more error-prone than a stand-alone CMM in a controlled environment.
The choice should depend on measurement details, environment, part cost and risk.

answer.content: The document describes limited benefits of OMM: OMM may be performed on certain part features/characteristics while an off-machine post-process measurement may still be needed when the cost of a faulty part is sufficiently high[2]; if on-machine probing on the first part gives results within a percentage of the tolerance zone—often 10%—of measurements from an accurate CMM in an environmentally controlled room, future parts can be validated with probe on machine[4]; and removal of swarf and cutting fluid has been successful with various cleaning systems and techniques, such as tombstone fixtures and part cleaning baths[1]. Limitations compared with a stand-alone CMM: OMMs are generally more error-prone than measurements on a stand-alone CMM in an environmentally controlled area[1]; the machining environment has widely varying and uncertain temperature, humidity, and particulate matter conditions that challenge accurate OMM, and controlling this variability can be difficult, costly, and/or time-consuming[1]; when a machine tool goes out of calibration for machining, it simultaneously goes out of calibration for measurement[1]. The document also lists arguments of suspicion: measuring with the same axes, spindle, and frame used for machining; OMM being non-value-added and reducing productivity; probing routines being difficult and time-consuming to write; and the machine tool environment being unstable and unpredictable in humidity, temperature, cutting fluid, and swarf[8].

question.question: Describe the adaptive machining sequence in Section 6.3.7 that uses a probe on the machine tool spindle.
expected_points: Cut the part to an interim or near-finished shape.
Probe the semi-finish cut using the spindle probe.
Adjust machine offsets for part deflection, tool deflection, tool wear and other factors.
Bring the part into tolerance with a final cut.

answer.content: Section 6.3.7 covers on-machine, in-process-intermittent measurement of features with a probe on a CNC machine tool spindle [2]. In the adaptive machining use case, measurements are made after preliminary cutting, with example sequences “cut/measure/final cut” or “cut/measure/finish cut/measure/final cut” [3]. The described operations are: cut the part to some shape, which may be an interim part close to finished size or an unplanned interim part requiring an unscheduled measurement such as for a broken tool bit; probe the semi-finish cut with a probe on the machine tool spindle; adjust machine offsets for part deflections, tool deflections, tool wear, and other factors; then, after adjusting offsets, bring the part into tolerance with a final cut [1].

question.question: 根据文档，机床测量如何减少二次装夹问题，并在什么条件下可能改善产品质量？
expected_points: 机床测量避免把工件移到 CMM 时产生的二次装夹问题。
在测量足够准确且测量成本低于缺陷零件成本时，可能改善质量、客户满意度和盈利能力。
机床几何精度必须足以满足零件公差，并需要持续监控和校准。
